nameStory: The Cuban Brown Snail gets its name from its native homeland of Cuba, where it originally lived before spreading to other warm regions. The 'brown' part refers to its typical earthy shell coloration that helps it blend in with soil and leaf litter. Like many invasive species, it carries the name of its origin even as it establishes itself far from home.
description: The Cuban Brown Snail is a medium-sized land snail that breathes air rather than living in water. It has a rounded, spiral shell that's typically brown or tan in color, helping it blend into the forest floor. These snails are part of a group called terrestrial gastropods, which simply means they're belly-footed creatures that live on land. Though originally from Cuba, this species has spread to other areas and is considered a serious agricultural and ecological threat.

idTips.label: Shell shape and color
idTips.description: Look for a rounded, spiral shell with a brown to tan coloration that feels smooth to the touch when clean, though it may be covered with dirt or debris in the wild

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Medium-sized for a land snail, noticeably larger than the tiny snails you might find in your garden but smaller than large native species

idTips.label: Habitat preference
idTips.description: Often found in areas with rich, moist soil and organic matter where they can easily glide along on their muscular foot

idTips.label: Air-breathing behavior
idTips.description: Unlike aquatic snails, you'll never find these in water - they live entirely on land and breathe air through a small opening in their shell

habitat: In New England, Cuban Brown Snails would likely be found in warm, protected areas with rich, moist soil such as greenhouses, botanical gardens, or areas around heated buildings. They prefer locations with plenty of organic matter like compost piles, leaf litter, or well-mulched garden beds. Given their tropical origin, they would struggle in New England's harsh winters and might only survive in artificially warmed environments.

seasonality.spring: Most active as temperatures warm up, emerging from winter shelter to feed on fresh plant matter and organic debris.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they feed, grow, and reproduce most actively in warm, humid conditions.
seasonality.fall: Activity slows as they prepare for winter, seeking protected areas and reducing feeding as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Largely inactive or dead in New England's harsh winters, unless in heated indoor environments like greenhouses.

funFact: This humble-looking snail is considered such a serious agricultural threat that it's been recommended for 'top national quarantine significance' in the United States - meaning it could potentially cause millions of dollars in crop damage if it becomes widely established!
confusionNotes: Cuban Brown Snails might be confused with native New England land snails, but most of our native species are much smaller and adapted to cold winters. Memory trick: if you find a medium to large land snail in New England, especially near human activity or heated areas, it's more likely to be an introduced species than a native one.
contextualKnowledge: Despite having only one recorded observation in New England, this species represents the kind of 'sleeper' invasive that could establish itself through plant trade, greenhouse escapes, or warming temperatures due to climate change. Many destructive invasives start with just a few individuals in seemingly unsuitable habitat.
compareHints: The Cuban Brown Snail is the only member of its genus (Zachrysia) recorded in New England, making it unique among our land snails. Unlike many of our smaller native land snails that are adapted to cold winters, this tropical species would struggle to survive New England's climate without human-created warm microclimates. Its medium size and brown coloration distinguish it from most native species, which tend to be much smaller.
